title: Chapter 75 — The Right Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Now let's cross the deck and take a good long look at the Right Whale's head.

As in general shape the noble Sperm Whale's head may be compared to a Roman war-chariot (especially in front, where it is so broadly rounded), so, seen broadly, the Right Whale's head bears a rather inelegant resemblance to a gigantic galliot-toed shoe, its toe rounded like the bow of a Dutch galliot. Two hundred years ago an old Dutch voyager likened its shape to that of a shoemaker's last. And in this same last or shoe, that old woman of the nursery tale, with her swarming brood, might very comfortably be housed, she and all her children.

But as you get closer to this great head, it takes on different appearances depending on where you stand. If you stand on top of it and look at these two F-shaped spout-holes, you would think the whole head was an enormous bass-viol and these spiracles the holes in its sounding-board. Then again, if you fix your eye on this strange crested, comb-like crust on top of the mass — this green, barnacled growth that the Greenlanders call the Right Whale's "crown" and the Southern whalemen its "bonnet" — if you look only at this, you would take the head for the trunk of some huge oak with a bird's nest in its fork. At any rate, when you watch those live crabs nesting here on the bonnet, that idea is almost bound to occur to you — unless, of course, your imagination has latched onto the technical term "crown" that it also goes by. In that case you will find it very interesting to think that this mighty monster is really a crowned king of the sea, whose green crown has been assembled for him in this marvelous way. But if this whale is a king, he is a very sulky-looking fellow to grace a diadem. Look at that drooping lower lip! What an enormous sulk and pout! A sulk and pout that measures, by carpenter's rule, about twenty feet long and five feet deep — a sulk and pout that will give you some 500 gallons of oil and more.

A great pity, now, that this unfortunate whale should be hare-lipped. The cleft is about a foot across. Probably the mother, during an important interval, was sailing down the Peruvian coast when earthquakes made the beach gape. Over this lip, as over a slippery threshold, we now slide into the mouth. Upon my word, if I were at Mackinaw, I should take this for the inside of an Indian wigwam. Good Lord! Is this the road that Jonah went? The roof is about twelve feet high, and runs up to a pretty sharp angle, as if there were a regular ridge-pole there; while these ribbed, arched, hairy sides present us with those wondrous, half-vertical, scimitar-shaped slats of whalebone, say three hundred on a side, which, hanging down from the upper part of the head or crown bone, form those Venetian blinds that have been briefly mentioned elsewhere. The edges of these bones are fringed with hairy fibers, through which the Right Whale strains the water, and in whose tangles he keeps back the small fish when he goes open-mouthed through the seas of brit at feeding time. In the central blinds of bone, as they stand in their natural order, there are certain curious marks, curves, hollows and ridges, by which some whalemen calculate the creature's age, as the age of an oak is reckoned by its circular rings. Though the certainty of this test is far from demonstrable, it has the flavor of probability by analogy. At any rate, if we accept it, we must grant the Right Whale a far greater age than will seem reasonable at first glance.

In old times, the most curious fancies seem to have prevailed about these blinds. One voyager in Purchas calls them the wondrous "whiskers" inside the whale's mouth;* another, "hogs' bristles"; a third old gentleman in Hackluyt uses the following elegant language, with "chop" for jaw: "There are about two hundred and fifty fins growing on each side of his upper chop, which arch over his tongue on each side of his mouth."

*This reminds us that the Right Whale really does have a sort of whisker — or rather a mustache — made up of a few scattered white hairs on the upper part of the outer end of the lower jaw. These tufts sometimes lend his otherwise solemn face a rather bandit-like look.

As everyone knows, these same "hogs' bristles," "fins," "whiskers," "blinds," or whatever you please, supply the ladies with their busks and other stiffening contrivances. But in this respect the demand has long been declining. It was in Queen Anne's time that the bone was in its glory, the farthingale (a hooped petticoat) being then all the fashion. And as those ancient ladies moved about gaily, though in the jaws of the whale, as you might say, so, in a shower, with the same thoughtlessness, do we nowadays run under the same jaws for protection; the umbrella being a tent spread over the same bone.

But forget about blinds and whiskers for a moment now, and, standing inside the Right Whale's mouth, take a fresh look around you. With all these colonnades of bone arranged so neatly around you, wouldn't you think you were inside the great Haarlem organ, gazing at its thousand pipes? As a carpet for the organ, we have a rug of the softest Turkey weave — the tongue, which is stuck, so to speak, to the floor of the mouth. It is very fat and tender and tends to tear apart when it is hoisted on deck. As for this particular tongue in front of us, at a quick glance I'd call it a six-barreler — that is, it will yield about that much oil.

By now you must clearly see the truth of what I began with: that the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale have almost completely different heads. To sum up, then: the Right Whale's head has no great well of sperm, no ivory teeth at all, and no long, slender lower jawbone like the Sperm Whale's. The Sperm Whale, for his part, has none of those bony blinds, no huge lower lip, and hardly any tongue to speak of. And again, the Right Whale has two external spout-holes, while the Sperm Whale has only one.
Take your last look now at these venerable hooded heads while they still lie side by side; one will soon sink into the sea with no record kept, and the other will not be far behind.

Can you make out the expression on the Sperm Whale's head there? It is the one he died with, except that some of the longer wrinkles in his forehead now seem to have faded. To me his broad brow seems full of a prairie-like calm, born of a speculative indifference to death. But look at the other head's expression. See that astonishing lower lip, pressed by chance against the ship's side so that it hugs the jaw tightly. Doesn't this whole head seem to express an enormous practical resolve in the face of death? I take this Right Whale to have been a Stoic; the Sperm Whale, a Platonist, who might have taken up Spinoza in his later years.
